power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≥ .43", Text = "Support, perceived consensus, and expectation showed no condition effects (all p ≥ .43), and perceived momentum was slightly higher after the threat manipulation (p = .03; SI), so we pool across conditions."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≥ .43", "p = .28"), Sentence = c("Support, perceived consensus, and expectation showed no condition effects (all p ≥ .43), and perceived momentum was slightly higher after the threat manipulation (p = .03; SI), so we pool across conditions.", "Support did not differ meaningfully by party: 76.0% among voters of the governing TISZA party and 71.9% among voters of the former ruling party Fidesz (d = 0.07, Welch p = .28); an equivalence test places the difference within ±0.2 SD, a bound for a small effect set before testing (TOST p = .03; covariate models and by-party figures in SI, Table S3)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Industry leaders now ask for independent, pre-release safety testing of frontier AI systems; the US president dismissed such calls as fears about things that "won't happen."
What the public wants is well documented for the US and UK, but almost unknown elsewhere, and little is known about whether people believe their preference will be acted upon.
In a Hungarian online sample (n = 1,356), 75% supported mandatory independent safety testing before AI systems are released, regardless of partisanship.
Three in four also believed most Hungarians agree, and 61% believed that this majority was growing.
Yet only 32% expected such testing to be introduced.
In one of Europe's most polarized countries, AI safety regulation thus has a consensus but no champion.
The missing link is not a hidden majority but the belief that anyone will deliver it.

On 12 September 2026, the chief executive of Anthropic called for slowing frontier AI development and embedding independent third-party evaluators in AI labs; within a day, the heads of OpenAI and xAI publicly agreed.
The US president replied that "negative forces" were "bringing up things that won't happen" (1).
text.formatted: The US president replied that "negative forces" were "bringing up things that won't happen" <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Three executives and a president debated, on the public's behalf, whether the public needs protecting.
The public was not consulted.
Its view, however, is well documented.

In a 2025 probability-based US survey, 72% wanted independent experts to test AI systems before wide use, with near-identical shares among Democrats and Republicans (2); a review of 218 studies finds the same broad support, paired with low trust in either companies or governments to implement it (3).
text.formatted: In a 2025 probability-based US survey, 72% wanted independent experts to test AI systems before wide use, with near-identical shares among Democrats and Republicans (2); a review of 218 studies finds the same broad support, paired with low trust in either companies or governments to implement it <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Two gaps remain.
Nearly all evidence comes from the US and UK, where the issue is loudly contested.
EU member states now implementing the AI Act are largely unmeasured; in Hungary, as we describe below, the issue is not contested but surrounded by silence.
And surveys record only first-order preferences: that people want regulation, not whether they know others want it or expect to get it.

Beliefs about what others want matter because a policy demand becomes politically usable only when it is common knowledge: when people want a policy, know that others want it, and expect it to be acted on (4).
In the best-studied case, climate policy, the chain breaks at the second link, with majorities underestimating public support by nearly half (5).
text.formatted: In the best-studied case, climate policy, the chain breaks at the second link, with majorities underestimating public support by nearly half <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: For AI safety regulation in Hungary, we find a different break: the first two links hold, and the third is missing.
Hungary is among the most polarized political systems in Europe (7, 8), and nearly every policy question sorts along party lines (7).
text.formatted: Hungary is among the most polarized political systems in Europe <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8)</ref>, and nearly every policy question sorts along party lines <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: We surveyed four months after a change of government, when partisan sorting should be at its peak.
Hungary is therefore a demanding test of whether AI safety regulation can escape party lines.

It has adopted implementing legislation for the EU AI Act, but supervision sits inside the ministry that also promotes AI development, and the announced independent authority has not been created (9).
text.formatted: It has adopted implementing legislation for the EU AI Act, but supervision sits inside the ministry that also promotes AI development, and the announced independent authority has not been created <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: We measured each link: whether people want independent testing, whether they think others want it, whether they see that demand as growing, and whether they expect it to be delivered.
Five items on AI regulation (four analyzed here; the acquaintance estimate is in SI) closed a survey experiment on European identity (n = 1,356 analyzed respondents; see Methods).

Support, perceived consensus, and expectation showed no condition effects (all p ≥ .43), and perceived momentum was slightly higher after the threat manipulation (p = .03; SI), so we pool across conditions.
Demand.

75.3% (95% CI 73.1-77.6) agreed that AI developers should be required to undergo mandatory, independent safety testing before releasing a new system (M = 4.09 on 1-5); 5.7% disagreed and 41.9% strongly agreed (Fig. 1A).
text.formatted: 75.3% (95% CI 73.1-77.6) agreed that AI developers should be required to undergo mandatory, independent safety testing before releasing a new system (M = 4.09 on 1-5); 5.7% disagreed and 41.9% strongly agreed (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Support did not differ meaningfully by party: 76.0% among voters of the governing TISZA party and 71.9% among voters of the former ruling party Fidesz (d = 0.07, Welch p = .28); an equivalence test places the difference within ±0.2 SD, a bound for a small effect set before testing (TOST p = .03; covariate models and by-party figures in SI, Table S3).
text.formatted: Support did not differ meaningfully by party: 76.0% among voters of the governing TISZA party and 71.9% among voters of the former ruling party Fidesz (d = 0.07, Welch p = .28); an equivalence test places the difference within ±0.2 SD, a bound for a small effect set before testing (TOST p = .03; covariate models and by-party figures in SI, Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Known consensus.
Asked how many of 100 Hungarian adults agree, respondents estimated 69 on average (median 70; Fig. 1B); 74.8% placed the figure above 50 (81.7% of those who themselves agreed).
text.formatted: Asked how many of 100 Hungarian adults agree, respondents estimated 69 on average (median 70; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>); 74.8% placed the figure above 50 (81.7% of those who themselves agreed).

text.text: The mean estimate fell 6 points short of the observed rate (95% CI 4-9; SI).
The second link holds: supporters know they are a majority.
Perceived momentum.
60.6% believed the share of Hungarians wanting stricter AI rules had grown over the past two years, and only 9.5% believed it had shrunk (Fig. 1C).
text.formatted: 60.6% believed the share of Hungarians wanting stricter AI rules had grown over the past two years, and only 9.5% believed it had shrunk (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: Respondents thus perceived not only a majority but a growing one.
Missing delivery.
Only 32.3% (CI 29.8-34.9) thought mandatory testing was likely to be introduced in Hungary in the coming years; 23.4% thought it unlikely (Fig. 1D).
text.formatted: Only 32.3% (CI 29.8-34.9) thought mandatory testing was likely to be introduced in Hungary in the coming years; 23.4% thought it unlikely (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>).

text.text: Among supporters, 36.5% expected delivery.
Expectation was unrelated to age, sex, or education but was somewhat lower among Fidesz (former government) than among TISZA (current government) voters (28.8% vs.
35.1%, respectively) and higher with subjective social status (β = 0.12, p < .001)-the profile of trust in government, not of attitudes toward AI.
text.formatted: 35.1%, respectively) and higher with subjective social status (β = 0.12, p < .001)-the profile of trust in government, not of attitudes toward AI.

text.text: Perceived momentum was its strongest correlate (r = .30, vs. r = .16 for own support and perceived consensus).
Weighting to approximate the adult population on sex, age, and education left all estimates within 2 percentage points of the unweighted estimates (76.0%, 69.0, 32.4%).
Perceived likelihood that such testing will be introduced in Hungary in the coming years.
Scales in A, C, and D run from 1 to 5; percentages give the share responding 4 or 5; full item wording in SI.
Alt text: Four histograms.

Panels A and C are right-skewed toward agreement and perceived increase; panel B peaks between 70 and 90 with most estimates above 50; panel D peaks at the midpoint, with only a third in the likely range.
Hungarians want independent AI safety testing, know that most of their compatriots want it, and see demand as rising.
Pluralistic ignorance, unlike for climate policy (5), does not apply: in formal models it arises when beliefs about others lag behind changing attitudes (6), and here they did not lag.
What is missing is the last link: support does not translate into expectation.
Only a third expected mandatory testing to be introduced, a quarter did not, and the largest group was undecided.
The pattern is that of a valence issue (10): voters across parties agree on the goal, so parties can differ only in how credibly they are expected to deliver it.
text.formatted: The pattern is that of a valence issue <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>: voters across parties agree on the goal, so parties can differ only in how credibly they are expected to deliver it.

text.text: Accordingly, party affiliation predicted neither support nor perceived consensus, only expectations of delivery, and in the familiar direction: voters of the new government were more confident than those of the losing side (11).
text.formatted: Accordingly, party affiliation predicted neither support nor perceived consensus, only expectations of delivery, and in the familiar direction: voters of the new government were more confident than those of the losing side <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Respondents were judging the state as a regulator, not the technology; a single item cannot separate a judgment about AI regulation from generic pessimism about policy change.
Our data locate the gap; they do not explain it.
That judgment is well founded: in the United States the refusal was explicit (1).
In Hungary nobody refused, but no party has made it a visible issue either, and the regulators set up to implement the AI Act lack the independence the public wants (9).
text.formatted: In Hungary nobody refused, but no party has made it a visible issue either, and the regulators set up to implement the AI Act lack the independence the public wants <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Expectations settled at the level of generic trust in the state: the pattern of a consensus without a champion.
Politicians tend to underestimate public support for regulation (12); with no visible demand and nobody measuring it, the silence feeds itself.
text.formatted: Politicians tend to underestimate public support for regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>; with no visible demand and nobody measuring it, the silence feeds itself.

text.text: Two implications follow.
Correcting perceived norms, the standard remedy where consensus is hidden (5), would add little here: supporters already see themselves as a growing majority.
What is missing is the reverse transfer, from citizens to the politicians who would have to act.

In the seed-and-soil terms of wise interventions (13), the soil is unusually ready: citizens want independent testing and know they are a majority; the leading developers, whatever their motives, have asked for it themselves (1); and the EU AI Act already contains third-party conformity assessment for some high-risk systems.
text.formatted: In the seed-and-soil terms of wise interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>, the soil is unusually ready: citizens want independent testing and know they are a majority; the leading developers, whatever their motives, have asked for it themselves (1); and the EU AI Act already contains third-party conformity assessment for some high-risk systems.

text.text: The missing seed is a signal that carries an existing demand to those who tend to underestimate it (12).
text.formatted: The missing seed is a signal that carries an existing demand to those who tend to underestimate it <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: A politician would not have to create demand, only recognize it.
Three limitations.
First, the sample is a single online panel from one country, covering ages 18 to 69.

Second, the support item is one-sided: it asks whether companies should be required to test their systems, not what that would cost; the 75% shows that people want safety, not that they would accept every downside.

Third, we asked about the expected introduction of one policy only, so we cannot tell whether the low expectation is specific to AI or a general doubt that the state delivers; the same question about another popular policy would separate the two.
Data come from the final block of a preregistered survey experiment on European identity fielded in Hungary between 14 and 28 August 2026 by SEDO.
The AI items were not part of the preregistration; they were administered after all experimental manipulations and all preregistered outcome measures, immediately before the demographic block.
All analyses reported here are exploratory.

Respondents were recruited from an opt-in online panel with quotas set to Hungarian Central Statistical Office proportions for the population aged 18-69 on sex, age, education, and settlement type; they are not a probability sample.
Because quotas were filled at entry and the AI items came last, attrition shifted the analyzed sample's composition (women 60%); weighted estimates are reported in Results and SI.

Of 5,228 started sessions, 1,356 remained after quality exclusions and attrition (full chain in SI); the one in four who failed an attention check were retained, following the parent study's protocol (results without them in SI).
Item wording and full analytic details are in SI; confidence intervals are percentile bootstrap.
The study was approved by ELTE Eötvös Loránd University (approval 0286/2026), and all participants gave informed consent.
Data availability.
The reduced dataset, codebook, R analysis script, Figure 1 file, and Supporting Information are deposited on the Open Science Framework [14] and are available for review.
text.formatted: The reduced dataset, codebook, R analysis script, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> file, and Supporting Information are deposited on the Open Science Framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> and are available for review.

text.text: The project will be made public with a DOI upon acceptance.
Item wording in Hungarian and English is given in the Supporting Information.
Claude (Anthropic) was used to draft and edit text and to write analysis code; all analyses and text were verified by the authors.
Figure 1.
Demand, known consensus, perceived momentum, and expected delivery of mandatory independent AI safety testing in Hungary, August 2026 (n = 1,356).
(A) Agreement that AI developers should be required to undergo mandatory independent safety testing before releasing a new system.
(B) Estimated number of Hungarian adults out of 100 who agree with the statement in A; dashed line marks 50, solid line the observed rate (75%).
(C) Perceived two-year change in the share of Hungarians wanting stricter AI rules.
